history.q: What was the capital of the Aztec (Mexica) Empire, on whose site Mexico City was built?
history.fact: Founded around 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco, Tenochtitlan was linked to the shore by long causeways.

history.q: Which Spanish conquistador led the conquest of the Aztec Empire?
history.fact: Tenochtitlan fell in 1521 after a long siege in which Cortés relied heavily on Indigenous allies such as the Tlaxcalans.

history.q: Mexico's Independence Day commemorates the 1810 "Grito de Dolores," a call to arms by which priest?
history.fact: Every September 15 at night, Mexico's president reenacts the Grito from the National Palace balcony and rings the original Dolores bell.

history.q: The victory celebrated on Cinco de Mayo (5 May 1862) was won against the army of which country?
history.fact: Cinco de Mayo marks the Battle of Puebla; Mexico's Independence Day is actually celebrated on 16 September.

history.q: In what year did Mexico achieve independence from Spain?
history.fact: The Army of the Three Guarantees entered Mexico City in September 1821, and its leader Agustín de Iturbide was crowned emperor the following year.

history.q: Which long-ruling president was challenged by the Mexican Revolution that began in 1910?
history.fact: Díaz dominated Mexico for over three decades, a period known as the Porfiriato, before going into exile in Paris in 1911.

history.q: Which revolutionary leader from Morelos is most associated with the slogan "Tierra y Libertad" (Land and Liberty)?
history.fact: Zapata's Plan of Ayala (1911) demanded that land taken by large estates be returned to rural villages.

history.q: Which Maya city in the Yucatán is famous for the step pyramid El Castillo, the Temple of Kukulcán?
history.fact: At the spring and autumn equinoxes, shadows on El Castillo's stairway form the image of a serpent slithering down the pyramid.

history.q: Which 1848 treaty ended the Mexican-American War?
history.fact: Under the treaty, Mexico ceded roughly half of its territory, including present-day California, Nevada and Utah.

history.q: Which Austrian archduke was installed as Emperor of Mexico in 1864 with French backing?
history.fact: Maximilian was executed at Querétaro in 1867 after republican forces loyal to Benito Juárez regained control.

history.q: Which Aztec emperor ruled Tenochtitlan when Hernán Cortés arrived in 1519?
history.fact: Moctezuma received Cortés in Tenochtitlan in November 1519 and died in 1520 while held captive by the Spanish.

history.q: Which revolutionary leader led a 1916 raid on the town of Columbus, New Mexico?
history.fact: The US sent General John J. Pershing's Punitive Expedition into Mexico in response, but it never caught Villa.

history.q: Which ancient civilization carved the colossal stone heads found on Mexico's Gulf Coast?
history.fact: Seventeen colossal heads are known, each carved from a single basalt boulder; the largest stands about 3.4 m (11 ft) tall.

history.q: What was the Spanish colony that included Mexico called?
history.fact: At its height the Viceroyalty of New Spain stretched from Central America to present-day California and even governed the Philippines.

history.q: Which territory broke away from Mexico in 1836 and was annexed by the United States in 1845?
history.fact: For nearly a decade the independent Republic of Texas had its own president, currency and diplomatic representatives abroad.

history.q: Which Mexican general and president led the 1836 assault on the Alamo?
history.fact: Santa Anna dominated Mexican politics for decades and served as president on as many as 11 separate occasions.

history.q: Which priest took over leadership of the independence movement after Miguel Hidalgo's execution in 1811?
history.fact: His birthplace, Valladolid, the capital of Michoacán, was renamed Morelia in his honor in 1828.

history.q: Which former royalist officer was crowned Emperor of Mexico in 1822?
history.fact: His empire lasted less than a year: Iturbide abdicated in March 1823 and Mexico became a republic.

history.q: What name is given to the six young cadets who died defending Chapultepec Castle in 1847?
history.fact: A great white monument at the entrance to Chapultepec Park honors the six cadets, who are remembered every 13 September.

history.q: Which Maya city in Chiapas contains the tomb of the ruler Pakal the Great?
history.fact: Archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier found Pakal's tomb deep inside the Temple of the Inscriptions in 1952.

history.q: Which 1853-54 deal sold land in present-day southern Arizona and New Mexico from Mexico to the US?
history.fact: The US paid $10 million, largely to secure a flat southern route for a transcontinental railroad.

history.q: Which 1926-1929 uprising in central Mexico opposed the government's anticlerical laws?
history.fact: It ended in 1929 through agreements brokered with help from the US ambassador, Dwight Morrow.

history.q: Which 1838-39 conflict with France began partly over a French pastry cook's claim for damages?
choices: The War of the Triple Alliance
history.fact: Santa Anna lost a leg fighting the French at Veracruz in 1838 and later gave the leg a formal burial.

history.q: Who was the last Aztec emperor, captured by the Spanish when Tenochtitlan fell in 1521?
history.fact: Cortés had him executed in 1525; today Cuauhtémoc is honored as a symbol of Mexican resistance.

history.q: Who was the Indigenous woman who served as Hernán Cortés's interpreter during the conquest?
history.fact: Also known as Malintzin or Doña Marina, she spoke both Nahuatl and a Maya language, which made her invaluable to the Spanish.

technology.q: Which mathematical concept did the ancient Maya develop independently?
technology.fact: The Maya counted in base 20, writing numbers with dots and bars plus a shell-shaped symbol for zero.

technology.q: Which staple crop was first domesticated in what is now Mexico around 9,000 years ago?
technology.fact: Maize descends from teosinte, a wild grass native to the Balsas River valley in southern Mexico.

technology.q: Mexico is the world's largest producer of which precious metal?
technology.fact: Silver from mines in places like Zacatecas and Guanajuato helped make the Spanish "piece of eight" a global currency.

technology.q: The huge Pyramid of the Sun stands in which ancient city near Mexico City?
technology.fact: The name Teotihuacan was given by the Aztecs centuries after the city's decline and is often translated as "place where the gods were created."

technology.q: Which Mexican inventor patented an early color television system in 1940?
technology.fact: González Camarena was in his early twenties when he patented his color system in Mexico, and he later received a US patent for it too.

technology.q: Which Mexican scientist shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for research on ozone depletion?
technology.fact: Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland showed that CFC gases destroy stratospheric ozone, work that underpinned the 1987 Montreal Protocol.

technology.q: What were the farming plots, built on lake beds and still seen at Xochimilco, called?
technology.fact: Xochimilco's canals are part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, toured on colorful flat-bottomed boats called trajineras.

technology.q: Which state oil company was created after Mexico nationalized its oil industry in 1938?
technology.fact: President Lázaro Cárdenas expropriated foreign oil companies on 18 March 1938, a date still commemorated in Mexico.

technology.q: In 1951, Mexican chemist Luis E. Miramontes co-synthesized which compound, a key ingredient of early oral contraceptives?
technology.fact: The synthesis took place at the Syntex laboratories in Mexico City, working with Carl Djerassi and George Rosenkranz.

technology.q: Who became the first Mexican astronaut, flying aboard the Space Shuttle in 1985?
technology.fact: Aboard Atlantis on mission STS-61-B, Neri Vela helped deploy Mexico's Morelos II communications satellite.

technology.q: Chocolate comes from which plant, cultivated in Mesoamerica for thousands of years?
technology.fact: The Aztecs valued cacao beans so highly that they used them as currency.

technology.q: Mexico is the world's largest producer of which fruit, the main ingredient of guacamole?
technology.fact: Most of Mexico's avocados are grown in the volcanic highlands of Michoacán.

technology.q: The famous "Sun Stone" (Piedra del Sol) was carved by which civilization?
technology.fact: The basalt disc weighs about 24 tonnes; it was rediscovered in 1790, buried beneath Mexico City's main square.

technology.q: Which German automaker built the classic Beetle at its plant in Puebla until 2003?
technology.fact: The last original Beetle rolled off the Puebla assembly line in July 2003; in Mexico the car is affectionately called the "vocho."

technology.q: The Dresden Codex, one of the few surviving pre-Columbian books, was made by which civilization?
technology.fact: Spanish friars burned most Maya books; only four Maya codices are known to survive.

technology.q: More than 3,000 years ago, Mesoamerican peoples made bouncing balls for their ritual ballgame from what?
technology.fact: The name "Olmec" comes from a Nahuatl word meaning "rubber people."

technology.q: Which round building at Chichén Itzá is believed to have served as an astronomical observatory?
technology.fact: Its windows are thought to align with key positions of Venus, a planet central to Maya calendars.

technology.q: Which Mexico City skyscraper, completed in 1956, was an early earthquake-resistant tower that survived the 1957 and 1985 quakes?
technology.fact: The tower rests on deep concrete piles driven into the soft clay of the old lakebed beneath the city.

technology.q: What number base did the Maya use for counting?
technology.fact: Maya numbers were written with dots for one, bars for five and a shell symbol for zero.

technology.q: Alongside maize and squash, which crop domesticated in Mesoamerica completes the "Three Sisters"?
technology.fact: Maize stalks support the climbing beans, beans enrich the soil with nitrogen, and squash leaves shade out weeds.

technology.q: The Large Millimeter Telescope, a 50 m radio dish, stands atop which Mexican volcano?
technology.fact: Built with the University of Massachusetts, it is among the world's largest single-dish telescopes for millimeter waves.

technology.q: Which research center near Mexico City grew out of Norman Borlaug's wheat-breeding work?
technology.fact: Borlaug's high-yield wheat, developed in Mexico, helped spark the Green Revolution and won him the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize.

technology.q: Which chemical element did Andrés Manuel del Río discover in Mexico in 1801?
technology.fact: Del Río called it "erythronium," but doubts were raised; it was rediscovered in Sweden in 1830 and named vanadium.

technology.q: Which Zapotec capital in Oaxaca was built on an artificially leveled mountaintop?
technology.fact: Founded around 500 BCE, it overlooks the Oaxaca Valley and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with the city of Oaxaca.

technology.q: Which ruler of Texcoco, also famed as a poet, designed a great dike in the 1440s to protect Tenochtitlan from floods?
technology.fact: The roughly 16 km dike also kept the lake's salty water away from the fresh water around Tenochtitlan.

art.q: Which Mexican painter is famous for her self-portraits and her Casa Azul (Blue House)?
art.fact: The Casa Azul in Coyoacán, Mexico City, where Kahlo was born and died, is now the Frida Kahlo Museum.

art.q: Which Mexican muralist was married (twice) to Frida Kahlo?
art.fact: Rivera's "Detroit Industry" murals (1932-33) at the Detroit Institute of Arts celebrate the city's auto workers.

art.q: Which traditional Mexican music ensemble features violins, trumpets and the deep-voiced guitarrón?
art.fact: UNESCO added mariachi to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2011.

art.q: What are the brightly painted, fantastical creature sculptures of Mexican folk art called?
art.fact: Artisan Pedro Linares is credited with creating the first alebrijes in Mexico City in the 1930s, inspired by a fever dream.

art.q: Which Mexican writer, author of "The Labyrinth of Solitude," won the 1990 Nobel Prize in Literature?
art.fact: Paz remains the only Mexican writer to have won the Nobel Prize in Literature; he also served as a diplomat in India.

art.q: Which 1955 novel by Juan Rulfo is set in the ghostly town of Comala?
art.fact: Gabriel García Márquez said Rulfo's short novel moved him so much that he could recite long passages of it by heart.

art.q: Which Mexican director won the Academy Award for Best Director for "Gravity" (2013)?
art.fact: Cuarón won Best Director again for "Roma" (2018), a black-and-white film set in Mexico City's Colonia Roma.

art.q: Which folk dance from Jalisco is known internationally as the "Mexican Hat Dance"?
art.fact: "Tapatío" refers to people from Guadalajara; dancers often wear the charro suit and the embroidered china poblana dress.

art.q: The elegant skeleton lady La Catrina originated in an etching by which Mexican printmaker?
art.fact: Posada called her "La Calavera Garbancera"; Diego Rivera later dressed and named her Catrina in his Alameda Park mural (1947).

art.q: Which Mexican architect, famous for bold colored walls, won the Pritzker Prize in 1980?
art.fact: Barragán's own house and studio in Mexico City was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004.

art.q: Which Mexican director won the Academy Award for Best Director for "The Shape of Water" (2017)?
art.fact: Del Toro is also known for "Pan's Labyrinth" (2006), which won three Oscars.

art.q: Which Mexican actress produced and starred in the 2002 biopic "Frida"?
art.fact: Her performance as Frida Kahlo earned her an Oscar nomination for Best Actress.

art.q: Which tin-glazed pottery, famous in Puebla, shares its name with a town in Spain?
art.fact: In 2019 UNESCO listed the Talavera craft of Puebla and Tlaxcala, together with that of Spain, as intangible cultural heritage.

art.q: What are the colorful perforated tissue-paper banners hung at Mexican fiestas called?
art.fact: Artisans traditionally cut dozens of layers of tissue paper at once using a hammer and small chisels.

art.q: Which art movement after the Revolution produced the public wall paintings of Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros?
art.fact: In the 1920s, education minister José Vasconcelos commissioned murals on public buildings to tell Mexico's history to all citizens.

art.q: Which muralist painted "Man of Fire" on the dome of Guadalajara's Hospicio Cabañas?
art.fact: The Hospicio Cabañas, a 19th-century orphanage filled with Orozco's murals, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.

art.q: Which writer wrote "The Death of Artemio Cruz" (1962)?
art.fact: Fuentes won the Cervantes Prize, the highest honor in Spanish-language literature, in 1987.

art.q: Which 17th-century nun and poet was called the "Tenth Muse"?
choices: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
art.fact: In her famous "Reply to Sister Philothea" (1691), she defended women's right to education.

art.q: Which Mexican director won back-to-back Best Director Oscars for "Birdman" and "The Revenant"?
art.fact: He was only the third director to win the award two years running, after John Ford and Joseph L. Mankiewicz.

art.q: Which beloved singer and star of Mexico's Golden Age of cinema died in a 1957 plane crash?
art.fact: The crash happened in Mérida, Yucatán; his films such as "Nosotros los pobres" (1948) remain hugely popular.

art.q: Which Oaxaca-born painter, who has a museum named after him in Chapultepec Park, kept his distance from political muralism?
art.fact: The Museo Tamayo opened in 1981 to house the international modern art collection he donated to Mexico.

art.q: Juan O'Gorman covered which building at UNAM's main campus with a giant stone mosaic?
art.fact: The mosaic, made of colored stones gathered from across Mexico, covers about 4,000 m² of the library's walls.

art.q: Which 19th-century painter is celebrated for his panoramic landscapes of the Valley of Mexico?
art.fact: Velasco taught at the Academy of San Carlos, where a young Diego Rivera studied under him.

art.q: Which composer wrote "Huapango" (1941), a much-loved Mexican orchestral work?
art.fact: Based on folk sones from Veracruz, "Huapango" is often called Mexico's second national anthem.

art.q: Which author, winner of the 2013 Cervantes Prize, wrote "La noche de Tlatelolco" about the 1968 student massacre?
art.fact: Poniatowska was born in Paris in 1932 to a family descended from Polish nobility and moved to Mexico as a child.

politics.q: How long is a Mexican president's term in office?
politics.fact: Known as the "sexenio," the six-year term cannot be renewed: presidential re-election is barred by the constitution.

politics.q: Which Zapotec-born president led Mexico's liberal reforms and resistance to the French intervention?
politics.fact: Mexico's first Indigenous president, Juárez is remembered for the line "respect for the rights of others is peace."

politics.q: How is Mexico's system of government best described?
politics.fact: Mexico divides power among executive, legislative and judicial branches, and among 31 states plus Mexico City.

politics.q: Which historic building on Mexico City's main square, the Zócalo, houses the offices of the federal executive?
politics.fact: The National Palace stands on part of the site of Moctezuma's palace, and its main staircase displays Diego Rivera's epic mural of Mexican history.

politics.q: What is the name of Mexico's two-chamber federal legislature?
politics.fact: It consists of a 500-seat Chamber of Deputies and a 128-seat Senate.

politics.q: Mexico's current constitution was adopted in which year?
politics.fact: Signed in Querétaro on 5 February 1917, it was among the first constitutions to guarantee social rights such as labor protections.

politics.q: Which party lost the presidency in 2000 after holding it continuously for 71 years?
politics.fact: Founded in 1929 as the PNR, the party took the PRI name in 1946; its run ended with the election of the PAN's Vicente Fox.

politics.q: What is Mexico's official name?
politics.fact: In Spanish it is "Estados Unidos Mexicanos," reflecting the country's federal union of states.

politics.q: Under which president did Mexican women win the right to vote in federal elections in 1953?
politics.fact: Mexican women voted in a federal election for the first time in 1955.

politics.q: Which leader popularized the slogan "Sufragio efectivo, no reelección" when challenging Porfirio Díaz in 1910?
politics.fact: Madero became president in 1911 but was overthrown and killed in 1913 during the "Decena Trágica" (Ten Tragic Days).

politics.q: Which former Coca-Cola executive served as Mexico's president from 2000 to 2006?
politics.fact: Fox rose to head Coca-Cola's operations in Mexico and later served as governor of Guanajuato before winning the presidency.

politics.q: How many terms may a Mexican president serve?
politics.fact: The ban on reelection, a legacy of the Revolution, is lifelong: no one who has held the office may ever hold it again.

politics.q: Which trade agreement among Mexico, the United States and Canada took effect in 1994?
politics.fact: It created one of the world's largest free-trade areas, phasing out most tariffs among the three countries.

politics.q: Which president nationalized Mexico's oil industry in 1938?
politics.fact: Cárdenas also carried out sweeping land reform, distributing millions of hectares to rural communities.

politics.q: What is the lower house of Mexico's Congress called?
politics.fact: It has 500 members: 300 elected in single-member districts and 200 chosen by proportional representation.

politics.q: Which party, registered in 2014, carried Andrés Manuel López Obrador to the presidency in 2018?
politics.fact: López Obrador won the 2018 election with about 53% of the vote.

politics.q: Not counting Mexico City, how many states does Mexico have?
politics.fact: Mexico City, long known as the Federal District, became a federal entity of its own in 2016.

politics.q: Which president launched a military offensive against drug cartels in December 2006?
politics.fact: Within days of taking office, Calderón sent thousands of troops and federal police to his home state of Michoacán.

politics.q: Which president, elected in 2012, returned the PRI to power after 12 years in opposition?
politics.fact: His "Pact for Mexico" with the main opposition parties produced reforms in energy, education and telecommunications.

politics.q: What is the name of Mexico's autonomous body that organizes federal elections?
politics.fact: The voter ID card it issues is the most widely used form of official identification in Mexico.

politics.q: Days before the 1968 Olympics, troops opened fire on a student rally in which Mexico City square?
politics.fact: The Tlatelolco massacre took place on 2 October 1968; the exact death toll remains disputed.

politics.q: Which former president founded the National Revolutionary Party in 1929, the forerunner of the PRI?
politics.fact: Calles remained the power behind the presidency until 1934, a period known as the "Maximato."

politics.q: Which revolutionary leader called the convention that drafted Mexico's 1917 constitution?
politics.fact: Delegates met in Querétaro; the 1917 text was among the first in the world to enshrine workers' social rights.

politics.q: How many members sit in Mexico's Senate?
politics.fact: Each state and Mexico City elect three senators, and the remaining 32 are chosen from national party lists.

politics.q: Which group launched an armed uprising in Chiapas on 1 January 1994?
politics.fact: Named after Emiliano Zapata, it rose up on the day NAFTA took effect; its masked spokesman, Subcomandante Marcos, became world famous.

current-affairs.q: Who was elected Mexico's first female president in June 2024?
current-affairs.fact: A former mayor of Mexico City, Sheinbaum also holds a PhD in energy engineering.

current-affairs.q: Which president did Claudia Sheinbaum succeed when she took office on 1 October 2024?
current-affairs.fact: López Obrador, president from 2018 to 2024, is widely known by his initials, AMLO.

current-affairs.q: Which Mexican boxer became the first undisputed super middleweight world champion in November 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Nicknamed "Canelo" (cinnamon) for his red hair, Álvarez collected all four major belts by beating Caleb Plant in Las Vegas.

current-affairs.q: Which rail project, whose first section opened in December 2023, loops through the Yucatán Peninsula?
current-affairs.fact: Its roughly 1,550 km route links Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo, passing near Maya archaeological sites.

current-affairs.q: Which hurricane struck Acapulco as a Category 5 storm in October 2023?
current-affairs.fact: Otis exploded from a tropical storm into a Category 5 hurricane in roughly a day, leaving little time to prepare.

current-affairs.q: Which Mexico City stadium was chosen in 2024 to host the opening match of the 2026 FIFA World Cup?
current-affairs.fact: Estadio Azteca hosted the 1970 and 1986 World Cup finals, and in June 2026 it became the first stadium to stage matches at three men's World Cups.

current-affairs.q: Under a constitutional reform approved in 2024, how are Mexico's federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, chosen?
choices: Appointed for life by the president
Selected by a national bar exam
current-affairs.fact: Mexico held its first nationwide judicial elections in June 2025.

current-affairs.q: Which Mexican driver finished runner-up in the 2023 Formula One World Drivers' Championship?
current-affairs.fact: "Checo" Pérez's second place behind teammate Max Verstappen was the best F1 championship finish ever by a Mexican driver.

current-affairs.q: Which international airport near Mexico City opened in March 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Built at the Santa Lucía air base, the airport is named after Felipe Ángeles, a general of the Mexican Revolution.

current-affairs.q: In 2022, Mexico reserved the exploitation of which mineral to the state, creating the company LitioMx?
current-affairs.fact: Lithium is a key ingredient in rechargeable batteries for phones and electric cars.

current-affairs.q: Which black-and-white film won Alfonso Cuarón the Oscar for Best Director in February 2019?
current-affairs.fact: Named after Mexico City's Colonia Roma, it also won Best Foreign Language Film, a first for Mexico.

current-affairs.q: Before winning the presidency, Claudia Sheinbaum served from 2018 to 2023 as head of government of which city?
current-affairs.fact: Sheinbaum is also a scientist with a PhD in energy engineering who contributed to reports of the UN's climate panel, the IPCC.

current-affairs.q: Which trade agreement replaced NAFTA when it entered into force in July 2020?
current-affairs.fact: Known in Mexico as T-MEC, it updated NAFTA with new rules on car parts, labor rights and digital trade.

current-affairs.q: Which Mexican drug lord was convicted by a US federal jury in New York in February 2019?
current-affairs.fact: He was sentenced to life in prison plus 30 years and is held at the ADX Florence supermax prison in Colorado.

current-affairs.q: Which volcano near Mexico City erupted repeatedly in May 2023, briefly closing nearby airports?
current-affairs.fact: Its name means "Smoking Mountain" in Nahuatl; at about 5,400 m it is Mexico's second-highest peak.

current-affairs.q: Which new national security force did Mexico create in 2019?
current-affairs.fact: It absorbed the Federal Police, which was dissolved; a 2024 reform placed the Guard under the Defense Ministry.

current-affairs.q: Who finished second to Claudia Sheinbaum in Mexico's June 2024 presidential election?
current-affairs.fact: Gálvez, a senator and engineer of Otomí heritage, ran for an opposition coalition of the PAN, PRI and PRD.

current-affairs.q: In June 2022, Katya Echazarreta became the first Mexican-born woman in space aboard a rocket from which company?
current-affairs.fact: The electrical engineer flew on a suborbital New Shepard flight from West Texas.

current-affairs.q: In June 2019, Andy Ruiz Jr. became the first boxer of Mexican descent to win a world heavyweight title by beating whom?
current-affairs.fact: Ruiz, born in California to Mexican parents, won by seventh-round stoppage at Madison Square Garden.

current-affairs.q: Which former Bolivian president received political asylum in Mexico in November 2019?
current-affairs.fact: Morales stayed in Mexico only about a month before moving on to Argentina in December 2019.

current-affairs.q: Which new Pemex oil refinery in Paraíso, Tabasco, was inaugurated in July 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Tabasco, where the refinery was built, is the home state of then-president Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

current-affairs.q: Mexico won the 2023 CONCACAF Gold Cup by beating which team in the final?
current-affairs.fact: Santiago Giménez scored the only goal at SoFi Stadium near Los Angeles, giving Mexico a record ninth Gold Cup title.

current-affairs.q: A 2019 constitutional reform in Mexico required what across all branches and levels of government?
current-affairs.fact: Known as "parity in everything," it covers cabinets, courts, legislatures and candidacies at every level of government.

current-affairs.q: A constitutional reform approved in late 2024 abolished which Mexican autonomous transparency and data-protection institute?
current-affairs.fact: Its duties were transferred to government bodies, including a new Anti-Corruption and Good Government ministry.

current-affairs.q: Which historic airline was relaunched in December 2023 as a state-owned carrier run by the armed forces?
current-affairs.fact: The original Mexicana, founded in 1921, was one of the world's oldest airlines before it stopped flying in 2010.

general.q: What is the capital of Mexico?
general.fact: Sitting about 2,240 m above sea level, Mexico City is built largely on the drained bed of Lake Texcoco.

general.q: On Mexico's flag, what is the eagle perched on a cactus holding in its beak?
general.fact: It recalls the legend that the Mexica would found their city where they saw an eagle on a cactus devouring a serpent.

general.q: Which spirit is distilled from blue agave and named after a town in Jalisco?
general.fact: By law, tequila can only be made in Jalisco and designated areas of four other states: Guanajuato, Michoacán, Nayarit and Tamaulipas.

general.q: Which holiday on 1-2 November honors deceased loved ones with altars called ofrendas?
general.fact: Bright orange cempasúchil (marigold) petals are scattered to guide spirits home with their color and scent.

general.q: Which body of water separates the Baja California peninsula from mainland Mexico?
general.fact: Also called the Sea of Cortés, it is so rich in marine life that it is often nicknamed "the world's aquarium."

general.q: Which is the most widely spoken Indigenous language in Mexico?
general.fact: English words such as chocolate, tomato, avocado and coyote all come from Nahuatl.

general.q: Which rich sauce from Puebla famously combines chili peppers with chocolate?
general.fact: Traditional mole poblano recipes can call for more than 20 ingredients, including several kinds of dried chili.

general.q: The beach resort of Cancún is in which Mexican state?
general.fact: Cancún was developed from a sparsely populated barrier island starting in 1970 as a government-planned tourism project.

general.q: Which Mexican monument is the largest pyramid in the world by volume?
general.fact: Overgrown so thoroughly it looks like a hill, the Cholula pyramid has a Spanish colonial church perched on top.

general.q: What is Mexico's highest mountain?
general.fact: Also called Citlaltépetl, Pico de Orizaba (about 5,636 m) is North America's highest volcano and third-highest peak.

general.q: What is the name of Mexico's currency?
general.fact: The "$" sign is thought to have originated as a symbol for the peso, centuries before the US dollar adopted it.

general.q: What is the candy-filled figure that blindfolded children break with a stick at Mexican parties?
general.fact: Piñatas are traditional at the Christmas-season Posadas; the classic seven-pointed star is said to represent the seven deadly sins.

general.q: What is Mexico's most popular sport?
general.fact: Mexico hosted the men's World Cup in 1970 and 1986; co-hosting in 2026 makes it the first country to host three.

general.q: The city of Mérida is the capital of a state on which peninsula?
general.fact: The Yucatán Peninsula separates the Gulf of Mexico from the Caribbean Sea.

general.q: Which thin flatbread made from corn or wheat is the base of tacos?
general.fact: Corn tortillas use nixtamalized maize, soaked in limewater, an ancient technique that makes the corn more nutritious.

general.q: Tacos al pastor were inspired by the spit-roasted meat brought by immigrants from which country?
general.fact: In Puebla, "tacos árabes" served in pita-style bread preserve an earlier form of the dish.

general.q: In which year did Mexico City host the Summer Olympics?
general.fact: The thin air at altitude is often credited with aiding Bob Beamon's long jump of 8.90 m, a world record that stood for nearly 23 years.

general.q: What are the natural limestone sinkholes of the Yucatán, sacred to the Maya, called?
general.fact: Many cenotes connect to vast flooded cave systems; Sac Actun near Tulum is among the longest known underwater caves.

general.q: Which milky alcoholic drink, sacred to the Aztecs, is made by fermenting agave sap?
general.fact: In Aztec times pulque was linked to Mayahuel, goddess of the maguey plant, and its use was strictly regulated.

general.q: Which masked lucha libre wrestler starred in dozens of films and became a Mexican icon?
general.fact: El Santo kept his identity hidden for decades and was buried wearing his famous silver mask in 1984.

general.q: Which is Mexico's largest state by area?
general.fact: Chihuahua's Copper Canyon system is larger than the Grand Canyon, with some gorges even deeper.

general.q: On which tree do millions of monarch butterflies cluster in their Mexican wintering grounds?
general.fact: The Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve in the mountains of central Mexico became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.

general.q: Which equestrian tradition, inscribed by UNESCO in 2016, is officially Mexico's national sport?
general.fact: Mariachi musicians perform in the traje de charro, the ornate horseman's suit of charrería.

general.q: In which city is the Guelaguetza, a July festival of regional dance, held?
general.fact: Delegations from across the state perform; the name comes from a Zapotec word for reciprocal giving.

general.q: Which tiny porpoise, the world's most endangered marine mammal, lives only in Mexico's northern Gulf of California?
general.fact: Its name means "little cow"; recent surveys have estimated only around ten individuals remain.
